extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers interested in philosophy of science and foundations of scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for how scientific inquiry should treat concepts like cause, force, and will — distinguishing descriptive laws from metaphysical explanations and advising inference grounded in experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics is descriptive, not metaphysical enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanics is 'the science of motion' whose object is 'the complete description in the simplest possible manner of such motions as occur in nature' (Kirchhoff).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mechanical 'explanations' as concise descriptions of routines of perception; do not contrast the 'mechanical' with the 'intellectual' as if mechanics imposes inherent necessity on nature. Recognize quantitative (simplicity, generality) rather than qualitative differences between branches (e.g., mechanics vs biology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific laws are intellectual products summarising routines of perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of mechanics (and other sciences) describe repeated sequences of sense-impressions and are 'essentially an intellectual product'; they do not provide a logical must or metaphysical enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret laws as summaries of past experience used to predict future experience (the how), not as answers to the metaphysical why. Resist attributing inherent necessity to laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force should not be treated as a metaphysical cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Force, if looked upon as a cause that necessitates a routine of perceptions, leads outside the scope of science; force is more properly a certain measure of change of motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid textbook or popular formulations that present force as an inherent agent in matter producing change; instead treat 'force' as a measure/description (e.g., the force of gravitation describes the rate at which motion is changed) and beware that using 'force' as a cause can mask ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish popular/metaphysical 'cause' from scientific 'cause'
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular usage often conceives 'cause' as enforcement or necessity (an agent that makes a stage follow), whereas scientific usage should treat 'cause' as marking a stage in a routine of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating explanations, ask whether 'cause' is being used to imply enforcement (metaphysical) or simply to denote a stage in observed routines; prefer the latter for scientific clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: First causes are illegitimate for science
rubrics_metrics.description: First causes (arbitrary originators that enforce sequences) have no existence for science; assertions of first causes indicate a limit of knowledge rather than valid scientific inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer 'first causes' from scientific investigation; where such assertions appear, treat them as markers of ignorance or metaphysical speculation. Follow the canon that one should not pass from the known to something totally unlike it in the unknown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Will is a secondary cause, not an enforcing first cause
rubrics_metrics.description: The will known to us is associated with consciousness and the physiological brain and appears, on analysis, as a stage in the routine of perceptions (a secondary cause) rather than an arbitrary first cause that enforces sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain actions attributed to 'will' in terms of stored impressions, memory, brain structure, heritage, training and experience. Do not posit will as a metaphysical enforcer; free-will, if real, is acting in accordance with individuality, not breaking mechanical causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary causes involve no enforcement; science describes how not why
rubrics_metrics.description: In secondary causes (stages following an initial act or in ordinary sequences) science finds no element of enforcement—only routines of experience which can be described mechanically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that science can describe the stages (how things change) but cannot, by such description alone, answer the metaphysical why. Example: Newton's law describes rates of fall, not why gravity exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference must be grounded in experience; avoid postulating unthinkable entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Passing beyond sense-impressions to unobservable or 'unthinkable' x, y, z (e.g., hidden forces or absolute will) is meaningless for scientific reasoning and constitutes illegitimate inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the canons of logical inference (e.g., avoid moving from known to something totally unlike it) and confine explanations to what can be inferred from experience. Where the routine cannot be traced further, acknowledge ignorance rather than invent first causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simpler, more general descriptions and assess probabilistically
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions that are simpler and more general (e.g., mechanical descriptions) are to be preferred because they cover more of our past experience; we should 'measure the amount of probability that one description... will ultimately be recognised as capable of replacing another.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing competing descriptions, weigh simplicity and generality and assess how probable it is that one description will supplant another based on empirical adequacy; this is a probabilistic, not categorical, judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not multiply causes unnecessarily (parsimony)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science should not 'unnecessarily multiplic[y] causes' when no simplification results from their postulation; invoking extra causes often masks ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer stating 'Here, for the present, our ignorance begins' over inventing first causes or metaphysical agents. Apply parsimony: postulate additional entities only when they simplify and improve empirical description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for apparent agency historically and psychologically
rubrics_metrics.description: Primitive and historical attributions of agency (sun-gods, storm-gods, will behind phenomena) arise from the early mental association of will with causation and from gaps in analysis; modern science progressively replaces these with descriptive accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encountering anthropomorphic or spiritualistic explanations, interpret them as historical/psychological fossils and seek mechanistic/descriptive accounts that replace supernatural agency as knowledge advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat mental individuality and brain mechanisms as describable links in causal routines
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in will and behaviour are linked to individual brain structure, heritage, training and experience; these are stages in routines that can, in principle, be mechanically described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating explanations of behaviour or volition, look for physiological, developmental, and environmental determinants rather than assuming irreducible psychical causes; recognise that fuller mechanistic description may convert apparent first causes into secondary causes.
